summary: A skeleton iron tower north of Hillsboro Inlet, lit in March 1907 to close the dark gap above the Florida reef; its Fresnel lens still turns, and visits are by boat tour.

access.note: Grounds closed to walk-in visitors; boat tours run by the Hillsboro Lighthouse Preservation Society from Pompano Beach on scheduled Saturdays; tower climbed on tour.

corrections.why: The record gives 1974; the Preservation Society gives 16 February 1979, consistent with the reference number 79000661.
The record's 1942 'built' event matches only the timer and generator building in the nomination; the tower dates from 1907.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give differing characteristics because the flash period changed from 10 to 20 seconds when the light was electrified in 1932 (Preservation Society); see notes.

notes_for_editor: Sources 2 (LighthouseFriends) and 4 (HLPS history) carry most of the 1907-2020 narrative and are secondary; the HLPS history cites station records but gives no page references, so its Berghell dispute, school, pay, dimming and relighting details are unverified against the originals. Many claims in the story are supported only there. The 1935 gale: the Bulletin issue (PDF p.4 of the 1936 volume) says 'last November', so November 1935; LighthouseFriends says 1936. Hurricane 1926: Bulletin gives 18 September, LighthouseFriends 19 September. The 1922 Commissioner report (fiscal year ended June 1922) gives the Tancrede/H. C. Folger/motor-boat rescues without dates. Tower height: 132 ft (NRHP), 137 ft (LF), 136/147 ft (HLPS); record says 42 m. The tower origin (Detroit contract vs. 1904 St. Louis exposition) is unresolved. Current characteristic Fl(2) W 20s in the record was not confirmed from a source; the HLPS says the period is 20 s. Tour season and fees change; check hillsborolighthouse.org. Coast Guard personnel after 1960 are not named in the story. Fact-check 2026-10-22: roster extended with the archive's pre-1960 lines (USCG-era names after 1959 left out under the living-people rule). 5.5 million candlepower: LighthouseFriends ties it to the 1932 electrification, the Society to a 1966 bulb change. Study recommending lens removal: 1993 per the Society, 1996 per LighthouseFriends. NRHP names Russell Wheel for the metal work and also the St. Louis exposition origin, so the nomination itself holds both accounts.
